messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At forty, Samir, a married paramedic of Syrian-American descent, had spent his life responding to others’ catastrophes until the coordinates led him to his own street, where his wife’s sedan had clipped a concrete barrier. He found her pinned, her face pale against the cracked windshield, a dark trail of blood pooling beneath her seat. When he cut the seatbelt and pulled her onto the asphalt, the sight of her mottled, tearing skin and the sharp, antiseptic tang of the ambulance bay bleeding into the scene froze him. The memory of that afternoon remains fractured; there are entire minutes he cannot recall, yet when the fragments surface, they flood back with the same paralyzing terror he felt when her chest stopped beating. That unremembered time fuels a quiet, corrosive certainty: he has permanently changed for the worse, and his hands can no longer be trusted to save the people he cares about. Because he believes he failed to protect her, he now scans every roadside scene for visible injuries with a sharp, anticipatory dread. Now, working his ambulance routes through the city, Samir finds the world relentlessly amplifying that dread. The sight of a bicyclist’s shattered knee instantly drags him back to the roadside, triggering a jolt of physiological alarm that mirrors his threat response. The vivid, multi-sensory flashbacks make him feel unmoored, so he begins to suppress his thoughts about the crash, forcing his attention onto the radio chatter. Yet the hospital smell from a recent call, trapped in his cab’s upholstery, quickly pierces through his efforts, pulling him back to the ER waiting room. The fragmented recall forces him to overwork, hoping the grueling hours will keep the suppressed memories at bay, but the sensory reliving triggers a jolt of alarm when his partner reaches to check his blood pressure. This constant startle response shatters his ability to concentrate on patient vitals, which makes him dread the next shift, so he starts avoiding critical paramedic training seminars. The pattern solidifies into a heavy, self-reinforcing rhythm. His conviction that he fundamentally cannot rely on himself drives him to throw himself into double shifts, but the overworking leaves him emotionally numb, which reinforces his belief that he has permanently changed for the worse. The gaps in his recollection make him doubt his own clinical judgment, which deepens his negative appraisals of his competence, which in turn makes him hyper-aware of hospital corridors, turning a simple supply run into a trigger. The exhaustion from overworking guarantees a drop in alertness, which leaves him startled by sudden sounds in the bay, which pushes him to seek out safe seats with his back to the wall, scanning every entrance. As the months passed, the loop tightened: his attempts to suppress the trauma only allowed victim memories to surface during quiet moments, which made him more startled by routine movements at work. The startle responses fractured his concentration further, which made him distrust his own clinical judgment, cementing his belief that he has permanently changed for the worse. Those appraisals made him hyper-aware of every wound he encountered, which triggered visceral flashbacks. The flashbacks brought back the terror, which made him seek out safe seats in the ambulance bay, which left him isolated and overworked. The avoidance of team briefings left him feeling like an outsider, which heightened his negative appraisals of his own competence, which in turn made him hyper-aware of hospital corridors, turning a simple supply run into a trigger. The jolt of physiological alarm leaves him hyper-vigilant, so he flinches at the sight of a child’s scraped elbow in a grocery aisle. Samir finally sought therapy because the double shifts were causing him to drop off a patient en route to the hospital, and he knew he could no longer afford another mistake. He is most afraid of losing control during an emergency or watching someone he loves slip away helplessly, but he hopes to reclaim his focus, sit without mapping exits, and look at a wound without seeing his wife’s face. He wants to trust his hands again, to remember without reliving, and to finally stop running from the very people he swore to protect.
